claim: Hives is listed with shingles, mumps and rabies as a singular noun in -s.
evidence_summary: Wiktionary codes hives as plural with singular hive, and shingles as uncountable. The OED entry hives, n. says “Chiefly with plural agreement”, but it dates from 1898, is not fully revised, carries a Scottish English label, and its one Hives are quotation is from an 1893 Northumberland glossary. An NHS page has hives keeps coming back (seen through a summary only).
finding: The evidence conflicts. Present-day agreement data (Hives is/are) in edited medical or general prose would decide whether hives belongs with hiccups in [42ii].
inference: Does hives pattern with shingles in requiring singular agreement?

evidence.passage: §3.2.3, p. 346 [42i]. “The terms in [i] are singular nouns, behaving like our model example shingles.”
evidence.establishes: A lead only. The dictionary classification is not agreement evidence.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.

evidence.example: hives: noun, plural, singular hive, “Itchy, swollen, red areas of the skin”. shingles: noun, uncountable, “Herpes zoster”.
evidence.establishes: The two nouns CGEL groups together receive different number codings.

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, “hives, n.” (first published 1898; not fully revised).
evidence.example: Sense a: “Chiefly with plural agreement.” Quotation 1893 (Heslop): Hives are not usually outward eruptions.
evidence.establishes: Historical and regional evidence for plural agreement. It does not establish present-day usage.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, sense a. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.
